record.context_brief: Randomness relative to a finite set
record.original_question: Let the degree of randomness of a finite string x be measured by comparing the complexity of x with the complexities of all strings of the same length. Extend this notion to randomness with respect to an arbitrary finite set M, in a way that respects the intuition that if M has m elements and admits a description whose length is negligible compared with log m, then almost all elements of M should have near-maximal complexity, close to log m, relative to M.

evidence.quote: 22. The degree of randomness of a string x depends upon the complexity of the string x compared with the complexities of all strings having the same length. Extend this definition of randomness "with respect to an arbitrary finite set". An appropriate solution should conform the following intuitive fact: if a finite set of strings M containing m elements, where m is very large, can be defined by a program of length negligible when compared with log m, then almost all elements of M should have maximal complexity (which is close to log m); these strings should be "random" with respect to M. (C. Calude)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite binary string $x \in \{0,1\}^*$, let $K(x)$ denote its (plain or prefix-free) Kolmogorov complexity, i.e., the length of a shortest program that, run on a fixed universal Turing machine, outputs $x$. The customary degree of randomness of a string $x$ of length $n$ is measured by comparing $K(x)$ with the complexities of all strings of length $n$ (equivalently, with $\log_2 2^n = n$): $x$ is called random when $K(x)$ is close to $n$.

Propose and justify a definition of the "degree of randomness of a string $x$ with respect to an arbitrary finite set $M \subseteq \{0,1\}^*$" (and, more generally, a notion of randomness of $x$ relative to $M$) that extends the classical notion (recovered when $M = \{0,1\}^n$) and that satisfies the following requirement:

If $M$ is a finite set with $m := |M|$ and $M$ admits a description (a program that enumerates or decides $M$) of length negligible compared with $\log_2 m$, then almost all elements $x \in M$ should be random with respect to $M$ under the proposed definition, in the sense that their complexity relative to $M$ is close to $\log_2 m$ (the maximal possible value up to an additive term that is small compared with $\log_2 m$).

Give a precise formal definition meeting this criterion, and prove the corresponding "almost all elements of an easily describable large set are random" theorem.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open problem (attributed to C. Calude) in a list of open problems in algorithmic information theory. Standard notions exist (e.g., conditional Kolmogorov complexity $K(x\mid M)$ and randomness deficiency $\log|M| - K(x\mid M)$ studied by Kolmogorov, Shen, Vereshchagin, Vyugin, and others), and these satisfy the stated intuitive property; however, whether any of these is regarded as a fully satisfactory "solution" to the problem as posed is not clearly established by the available sources. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

status_evidence.title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
status_evidence.snippet: Problem 22 (C. Calude): extend the definition of randomness with respect to an arbitrary finite set, conforming to the intuition that for easily describable large M, almost all elements should have complexity close to log m.
status_evidence.claim: The problem is listed among open problems in algorithmic information theory.
